fluid_dynamics.continuity.title: Continuity: volumetric and mass flow rate (Q = A·v)

fluid_dynamics.bernoulli_ideal.title: Bernoulli equation (ideal, along a streamline)
equations: p1 + rho*v1**2/2 + rho*g*z1 = p2 + rho*v2**2/2 + rho*g*z2
assumptions: Steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline; no shaft work or losses (for those, use the energy equation).

fluid_dynamics.energy_equation.title: Energy equation in head form (with losses and pump/turbine head)
assumptions: Steady, incompressible flow between two sections with uniform properties; the kinetic-energy correction factor α = 1. h_L bundles all friction and minor losses.
method_references: Extended Bernoulli / energy equation in head form

fluid_dynamics.jet_force.title: Force of a jet on a fixed vane (F = ρQv(1 − cos β))

variables.name: F
variables.desc: force on the vane in the jet direction

assumptions: Fixed vane, steady jet deflected through angle β from its original direction with no speed loss. β = 90° (flat plate) gives F = ρQv; β = 180° (cup) gives F = 2ρQv.

fluid_dynamics.momentum_bend.title: Force of a fluid stream on a pipe bend, nozzle or vane (2-D)

variables.name: Fx
variables.desc: x component of the force of the fluid on the bend

variables.name: Fy
variables.desc: y component of the force of the fluid on the bend

procedure.python:
def _momentum_bend(values):
    """Force of a steady fluid stream on a pipe bend/nozzle/vane (2-D, horizontal plane).

    inlet/outlet are [v (m/s), p (Pa, gauge), A (m²), theta (deg from +x)]; rho (kg/m³). The force is
    that exerted BY the fluid ON the bend: F = p1 A1 e1 − p2 A2 e2 + mdot (v1 e1 − v2 e2).
    """
    rho = values['rho']
    v1, p1, A1, th1 = map(float, values['inlet'])
    v2, p2, A2, th2 = map(float, values['outlet'])
    if A1 <= 0 or A2 <= 0:
        raise MechError('areas must be positive')
    # Steady incompressible flow: mass continuity requires A1·v1 = A2·v2.
    if abs(A1 * v1 - A2 * v2) > 0.01 * max(abs(A1 * v1), abs(A2 * v2), 1e-300):
        raise MechError('steady flow needs A1·v1 ≈ A2·v2 (continuity); these differ by more than 1 %')
    e1x, e1y = math.cos(math.radians(th1)), math.sin(math.radians(th1))
    e2x, e2y = math.cos(math.radians(th2)), math.sin(math.radians(th2))
    mdot = rho * A1 * v1
    Fx = p1 * A1 * e1x - p2 * A2 * e2x + mdot * (v1 * e1x - v2 * e2x)
    Fy = p1 * A1 * e1y - p2 * A2 * e2y + mdot * (v1 * e1y - v2 * e2y)
    return {'Fx': Fx, 'Fy': Fy, 'F': math.hypot(Fx, Fy), 'theta_F': math.atan2(Fy, Fx), 'mdot': mdot}

assumptions: Steady flow; the force reported is that exerted BY the fluid ON the bend (the anchoring force is equal and opposite). Steady flow requires ρ·A1·v1 = ρ·A2·v2; mdot uses the inlet values. Gauge pressures.
method_references: Control-volume momentum, F = p1A1e1 − p2A2e2 + ṁ(v1e1 − v2e2)

fluid_dynamics.turbine_torque.title: Euler turbomachine torque (T = ṁ(r₂v_t2 − r₁v_t1))

variables.name: T
variables.desc: torque on the fluid (negative for a turbine)

assumptions: T is the torque the fluid exerts on the rotor (Euler turbomachine equation). For a turbine the fluid loses angular momentum (r₂v_t2 < r₁v_t1), so T is negative; the shaft delivers the equal-and-opposite torque to the load. For a pump the signs reverse.

fluid_dynamics.sprinkler_torque.title: Rotating sprinkler arm torque (T = ρQr(v_j − ωr))

variables.name: v_j
variables.desc: jet velocity relative to the arm

assumptions: Two opposed jets at radius r; T is the torque needed to hold the rotation speed ω (T = 0 is the free-running speed ω = v_j/r).
method_references: Angular momentum of a rotating sprinkler

fluid_dynamics.strouhal_number.title: Strouhal number (St = fL/v)
assumptions: f is a cyclic frequency (Hz); angular frequencies must be converted first.

fluid_dynamics.hagen_poiseuille.title: Laminar pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille) and velocity profile
assumptions: Fully developed laminar flow (Re < 2300); parabolic profile u(r) = u_max(1 − (r/R)²) with u_max = 2·u_avg at the centreline.

fluid_dynamics.friction_factor.title: Darcy friction factor: laminar, Colebrook, Swamee–Jain, Haaland
assumptions: Use f_laminar for Re < 2300 and f_colebrook (or the closed forms) for Re > 4000; 2300 < Re < 4000 is transitional and uncertain. Below Re = 2300 the Colebrook/Swamee–Jain/Haaland correlations are turbulent relations and are misleading — use f_laminar there. Swamee–Jain is valid for 5000 < Re < 1e8 and 1e-6 < ε/D < 0.01; Haaland is an explicit fit accurate to ~2% of Colebrook.
method_references: Colebrook–White equation; Swamee–Jain (1976); Haaland (1983) explicit approximation

fluid_dynamics.head_loss.title: Major and minor head losses and equivalent length
assumptions: K is the tabulated minor-loss coefficient for the fitting (user input); equivalent length L_eq gives the same loss as the fitting at the same f.

fluid_dynamics.hydraulic_diameter.title: Hydraulic diameter for non-circular ducts (D_h = 4A/P)
assumptions: D_h substituted into Re and h_f relations approximates non-circular ducts (exact for a full circular pipe: D_h = D).

fluid_dynamics.series_pipes.title: Pipes in series: total head loss

variables.name: pipes
variables.desc: rows [L (m), D (m), f, K] for each pipe in series

variables.name: Q
variables.desc: common flow rate through all pipes

assumptions: Same flow rate through every pipe; losses add. Parallel pipes and general networks use the pipe-network (Hardy Cross) calculator.
method_references: Series pipe losses: h = Σ (f L/D + K) V²/(2g)

fluid_dynamics.pipe_network.title: Pipe network by the Hardy Cross loop method

variables.name: pipes
variables.desc: rows [id, L (m), D (m), f, K, Q0 (m³/s)]; Q0 satisfy junction continuity

variables.name: loops
variables.desc: [[[id, dir], ...], ...] with dir +1/−1 around each loop

variables.name: max_correction
variables.desc: largest loop flow correction of the last iteration

procedure.python:
def _pipe_network(values):
    """Pipe network by the Hardy Cross loop method.

    pipes: [[id, L (m), D (m), f, K, Q0 (m³/s)], ...]; initial flows Q0 must satisfy junction
    continuity. loops: [[[id, dir], ...], ...] with dir +1/−1 relative to each pipe's positive flow.
    Iterates ΔQ = −Σ(dr·R·Q|Q|) / Σ(2·R·|Q|) around each loop until |ΔQ| < 1e-9 m³/s.
    """
    pipes = values['pipes']
    loops = values['loops']
    idx, L, D, f, K, Q = {}, [], [], [], [], []
    for row in pipes:
        if len(row) != 6:
            raise MechError('pipes: each row must be [id, L (m), D (m), f, K, Q0 (m³/s)]')
        pid = row[0]
        idx[pid] = len(Q)
        L.append(float(row[1])); D.append(float(row[2])); f.append(float(row[3]))
        K.append(float(row[4])); Q.append(float(row[5]))
    n = len(Q)
    if n == 0:
        raise MechError('pipes: at least one pipe is required')
    A = [PI * d * d / 4.0 for d in D]
    R = [(f[i] * L[i] / D[i] + K[i]) / (2.0 * G0 * A[i] * A[i]) for i in range(n)]

    def resolve(pid):
        if pid not in idx:
            raise MechError(f'unknown pipe id {pid!r} in a loop')
        return idx[pid]

    it, maxcorr = 0, 0.0
    for it in range(1, 201):
        maxcorr = 0.0
        for loop in loops:
            num = den = 0.0
            entries = []
            for entry in loop:
                pid, dr = entry[0], (1.0 if float(entry[1]) > 0 else -1.0)
                i = resolve(pid)
                entries.append((i, dr))
                num += dr * R[i] * Q[i] * abs(Q[i])
                den += 2.0 * R[i] * abs(Q[i])
            if den == 0:
                continue
            dQ = -num / den
            maxcorr = max(maxcorr, abs(dQ))
            for i, dr in entries:
                Q[i] += dr * dQ
        if maxcorr < 1e-9:
            break
    if maxcorr >= 1e-9:
        raise MechError(f'Hardy Cross did not converge in 200 iterations (last |ΔQ| = {maxcorr:.3g} m³/s); '
                        'check the network definition and the initial flows')
    flows = [[pipes[i][0], Q[i], R[i] * Q[i] * abs(Q[i])] for i in range(n)]
    return {'flows': flows, 'iterations': it, 'max_correction': maxcorr}

assumptions: Hardy Cross loop balancing with fixed friction factors f and minor-loss K; initial flows must satisfy continuity at every junction (the corrections preserve it). Converges to Σh = 0 around each loop. f may be taken from the friction-factor calculator.
method_references: Hardy Cross method (1936) for pipe networks

fluid_dynamics.boundary_layer.title: Flat-plate boundary layer: thickness, displacement and momentum thickness

procedure.python:
def _boundary_layer(values):
    """Flat-plate boundary layer: laminar (Blasius) and turbulent (1/7 power law) thicknesses and C_f."""
    rho, U, x, mu = values['rho'], values['U'], values['x'], values['mu']
    if x <= 0 or mu <= 0:
        raise MechError('x and mu must be positive')
    Re_x = rho * U * x / mu
    if Re_x <= 0:
        raise MechError('Re_x must be positive (check the sign of U)')
    sx = math.sqrt(Re_x)
    delta_lam = 5.0 * x / sx
    dstar_lam = 1.7208 * x / sx
    theta_lam = 0.664 * x / sx
    cf_lam = 0.664 / sx
    cf_lam_mean = 1.328 / sx
    re15 = Re_x ** 0.2
    delta_turb = 0.37 * x / re15
    return {'Re_x': Re_x, 'delta_lam': delta_lam, 'delta_star_lam': dstar_lam, 'theta_lam': theta_lam,
            'delta_turb': delta_turb, 'delta_star_turb': delta_turb / 8.0, 'theta_turb': 7.0 * delta_turb / 72.0,
            'cf_lam': cf_lam, 'cf_turb': 0.0592 / re15,
            'cf_lam_mean': cf_lam_mean, 'cf_turb_mean': 0.074 / re15}

assumptions: Laminar: exact Blasius flat-plate solution (δ = 5.0x/√Re_x, δ* = 1.7208x/√Re_x, θ = 0.664x/√Re_x, local C_f = 0.664/√Re_x, mean C_f = 1.328/√Re_x). Turbulent: 1/7-power-law approximation (δ = 0.37x/Re_x^0.2, δ* = δ/8, θ = 7δ/72, local C_f = 0.0592/Re_x^0.2, mean C_f = 0.074/Re_x^0.2) for a smooth plate, Re_x up to ~1e7; constants vary slightly between texts. Transition near Re_x ≈ 5e5.
method_references: Blasius flat-plate solution; 1/7-power-law turbulent boundary layer

fluid_dynamics.drag_lift.title: Dynamic pressure, drag, lift and skin-friction force
assumptions: C_D, C_L and C_f are user inputs (from tables/data for the body shape and Re); A is the reference area appropriate to each coefficient. C_f is the mean (integrated) skin-friction coefficient over the wetted area.

fluid_dynamics.terminal_velocity.title: Terminal velocity of a falling body (v_t = √(2mg/(ρC_D A)))
assumptions: Drag balances weight (buoyancy neglected); constant C_D.
method_references: Terminal velocity from force balance mg = ½ρv²C_D A

fluid_dynamics.pitot_tube.title: Pitot tube velocity (v = √(2Δp/ρ))
assumptions: Incompressible flow; the stagnation point brings the fluid to rest isentropically.

fluid_dynamics.obstruction_flowmeter.title: Orifice / venturi / nozzle flow rate (Q = C_d A₂√(2Δp/(ρ(1−β⁴))))
assumptions: C_d accounts for losses and the vena-contracta (user input from meter tables); β = d/D is the diameter ratio.

fluid_dynamics.rotameter.title: Rotameter (variable-area meter) flow rate
assumptions: Float held up by drag against its buoyant weight; C_d is a user input.
method_references: Rotameter force balance Q = C_d (A_t − A_f) √(2gV_f(ρ_f − ρ)/(ρA_f))

fluid_dynamics.point_vortex.title: Point vortex: stream function and velocity potential
assumptions: 2-D point vortex at the origin; tangential velocity v_θ = Γ/(2πr) (see the circulation calculator) and vorticity is zero everywhere except at the origin (free vortex). With the stream function defined so that v_θ = −∂ψ/∂r, ψ = −(Γ/2π) ln(r/r0), fixed by ψ = 0 at r = r0; ψ is negative for r > r0 and positive for r < r0 (both signs are physical).
method_references: Point-vortex stream function and potential, ψ = −(Γ/2π) ln(r/r0)

fluid_dynamics.forced_vortex.title: Forced (solid-body rotation) vortex: velocity and vorticity
assumptions: Solid-body rotation: vorticity ζ = 2ω is uniform (radian is dimensionless, so 1 rad/s = 1 s⁻¹).

fluid_dynamics.circulation.title: Circulation (Γ = 2πr·v_θ)
method_references: Circulation Γ = 2πr·v_θ for an axisymmetric flow

fluid_dynamics.water_hammer.title: Water hammer pressure rise (Joukowsky)
assumptions: Sudden velocity change dV; elastic pipe (a rigid pipe is the limit E → ∞, c = √(K/ρ)). Joukowsky Δp = −ρ c dV is positive (a rise) for a sudden closure (dV < 0) and negative (a drop) for a sudden opening (dV > 0).
method_references: Joukowsky: Δp = −ρ c dV; elastic-pipe wave speed

fluid_dynamics.buckingham_pi.title: Buckingham π theorem: dimensionless groups from a dimension matrix

variables.name: matrix
variables.desc: rows = fundamental dimensions (M, L, T, …), columns = quantities, integer exponents; first `rank` columns are the repeating variables

variables.name: pi_groups
variables.desc: list of π groups (exponent vectors over the columns)

assumptions: The dimension matrix rows are the fundamental dimensions and columns the quantities; the first r columns must be independent repeating variables. Each π group = one non-repeating quantity times powers of the repeating variables (the nullspace of the matrix).
method_references: Buckingham π theorem (1914); nullspace of the dimension matrix

source.derivation: T = ṁ(r₂v_t2 − r₁v_t1) = 2(0.3·15 − 0.1·5) = 2(4.5 − 0.5) = 8 N·m (pump: angular momentum added to the fluid)
Turbine: the fluid loses angular momentum (r₂v_t2 = 0.1·5 = 0.5 < r₁v_t1 = 0.3·15 = 4.5). T = ṁ(r₂v_t2 − r₁v_t1) = 2(0.5 − 4.5) = −8 N·m, negative as expected for a turbine

f_laminar = 64/1e5 = 6.4e-4. Haaland: f = (−1.8 log10(0.001/3.7^1.11 + 6.9/1e5))⁻² = (−1.8·(−6.74717))⁻² = 0.0219662. Swamee–Jain: f = 0.25/log10(0.001/3.7 + 5.74/1e5^0.9)² = 0.25/3.34503² = 0.0223424. Colebrook: iterate 1/√f = −2 log10(0.001/3.7 + 2.51/(1e5·√f)) from the Haaland seed; converges to f = 0.0221745 (plain-math iteration, not mechcalc)
Inverse of the Colebrook case above: the relative roughness that gives f = 0.0221745 at Re = 1e5 is ε/D = 0.001

Γ = 2π. With v_θ = Γ/(2πr) and v_θ = −∂ψ/∂r, ψ = −(Γ/2π)·ln(r/r0) = −1·ln(2) = −0.693147 m²/s (negative for r > r0); φ = Γ/(2π)·θ = 1·0.5 = 0.5 m²/s. Numerical-derivative check at r = 2 m: dψ/dr ≈ [ψ(2+h) − ψ(2−h)]/(2h) with ψ(r) = −ln(r) and h = 1e-6 gives −dψ/dr = 0.5000 = Γ/(2πr) = v_θ, so the sign convention is consistent.

Sphere drag: columns [V, D, ρ, F, μ], rows [M, L, T]; rank 3, repeating variables V, D, ρ. π(F): solve D_r·a = −[1,1,−2]ᵀ: a_ρ = −1, a_V = −2, a_D = −2 → π1 = F·V⁻²D⁻²ρ⁻¹ = F/(ρV²D²) → exponents [−2,−2,−1,1,0]. π(μ): solve D_r·a = −[1,−1,−1]ᵀ: a = [−1,−1,−1] → π2 = μ/(ρVD) → exponents [−1,−1,−1,0,1] (inverse Reynolds number)
